elements.element: No non-compete restriction applies to Customer.
elements.evidence: Section 12.3 states that nothing restricts Customer from developing, acquiring, licensing, selling, or using any product or service and confirms that Customer made no non-compete commitment. Revised Section 12.4 affirmatively permits Customer to develop, market, sell, or acquire competing products or services.

elements.element: No field-of-use restriction applies to Customer.
elements.evidence: Section 12.3 expressly permits Customer to conduct business in any field or territory, and revised Section 12.4 permits competitive activity in any territory.

elements.element: Any restriction is limited to one specifically named competing product.
elements.evidence: No restriction remains, so there is no broader or unnamed-product restriction to limit.

elements.element: Any restriction applies during the term only.
elements.evidence: No restriction applies during or after the term; the original 24-month post-term restriction has been removed.

elements.element: Any restriction lasts no more than 12 months.
elements.evidence: No restriction or restricted period remains, so the 12-month maximum is not exceeded.

elements.element: Internal development is carved out from any restriction.
elements.evidence: Sections 12.3 and 12.4 affirmatively permit Customer to develop any product or service, including competing products, without excluding internal development.

elements.element: Acquisitions are carved out from any restriction.
elements.evidence: Sections 12.3 and 12.4 affirmatively permit Customer to acquire any product or service, including competing products.

result.reason: The operative language fully achieves the preferred position and therefore also satisfies the fallback limitations: Customer has no non-compete or field-of-use restriction, and development and acquisitions are expressly permitted. It preserves unrelated terms and removes the conflict between former Section 12.4 and Section 12.3. However, it is not strictly minimal because deleting Section 12.4 would have sufficed; the replacement provision substantially duplicates the broader protections already stated in Section 12.3.
